why_how.text: Every new Wisconsin driver passes the same short series of tests, so knowing the order removes surprises on test day.
The vision screening comes first because safe driving starts with seeing the road clearly.

scenario.text: Maya wears glasses and reads the acuity chart at twenty-forty with her left eye only.

reasoning.text: Acuity needs to reach twenty-forty in just one eye, and glasses are allowed for the reading.

result.text: Maya meets the acuity rule, and her field of vision is then measured from each eye.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking that wearing glasses fails the vision screening.

correction.text: Glasses or contacts are allowed, and the twenty-forty reading may be met with them on.

memory_support.text: Acuity one eye, field each eye.

prompt.text: Your cousin can read twenty-forty with one eye but not the other. Does that alone keep her from meeting the acuity rule?

answer.text: No. Acuity of at least twenty-forty is needed in only one eye.

rationale.text: The one-eye rule is for acuity; the separate seventy-degree field rule is the one measured from each eye.

lines.text: Four tests lead to a license.

narration.text: Welcome to your first lesson on getting a Wisconsin driver license. To drive on any public road in the state you need a valid license, and you earn it by passing a short series of tests. There is a vision screening, a highway signs test, a knowledge test about traffic laws, and a skills test where you actually drive. This lesson starts at the beginning of that line, with the vision screening: what it measures, who can give it, the two vision standards you must meet, and what happens next if you do not pass it the first time.

lines.text: Given by the DMV or your specialist.

narration.text: The vision screening measures how well you see. You do not have to visit a particular office for it: either the DMV can give the screening, or your own vision specialist can. That flexibility matters if you already see an eye doctor regularly. Whoever gives it, the screening checks two separate things, sharpness of vision and how wide your view is to the sides. Think of it as the gate before every other test, because the signs, knowledge and skills tests all assume you can see the road, the signs and other traffic clearly and early.

lines.text: Acuity at least twenty-forty in one eye.

narration.text: Regular car and motorcycle applicants must have visual acuity of at least twenty-forty, and that standard is met in one eye. Glasses or contacts are allowed while the reading is taken, so wearing them is not a problem. The second standard is field of vision, which is how much you can see to the sides while looking straight ahead. Applicants need a seventy-degree field of vision, measured from the center of each eye. Keep those two standards apart in your head: one is a sharpness rule for one eye, the other is a width rule checked for each eye.

lines.text: Field of vision: measured from each eye.

narration.text: Here is the trap in the vision rules. People remember that one of the standards is about a single eye and then attach that idea to the wrong rule. The acuity rule, at least twenty-forty, needs to be met in only one eye. The seventy-degree field-of-vision rule is the opposite kind: it is measured from the center of each eye. A test question may describe someone with one weak eye and ask whether they meet the acuity rule. The answer turns on which standard is being asked about, so slow down and match the eye count to the rule.

lines.text: See a vision specialist with the certificate.

narration.text: Failing the vision screening does not end your application. DMV staff explain the next step, which is a visit to a vision specialist. You bring along the Certificate of Vision Examination by Competent Authority, the form the specialist completes about your vision. So there are two different moments to keep straight. The first screening can be given by the DMV itself. After a failed screening, though, the next stop is a specialist with that certificate in hand. Knowing this in advance helps you plan, especially if you already have an eye doctor you can call.

lines.text: One weak eye: does acuity still pass?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: your cousin can read twenty-forty with one eye, but her other eye is weaker. Does that alone keep her from meeting the acuity rule? Work it out from the two standards in this lesson. The answer is no. Acuity of at least twenty-forty is needed in only one eye, and she may wear glasses or contacts for the reading. Her field of vision is a separate matter: that standard is seventy degrees, measured from the center of each eye, so she still has that part of the screening to pass. That is the difference between the two vision standards.

lines.text: Acuity one eye, field each eye.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. A Wisconsin license comes from passing four tests, and the vision screening is the first of them. The DMV or your own vision specialist can give it. You need acuity of at least twenty-forty in one eye, with glasses or contacts allowed, and a seventy-degree field of vision measured from the center of each eye. If you fail, staff explain that you visit a vision specialist with the vision certificate form. Next you will look at the highway signs test, the first of the two written tests on the path to your license.

why_how.text: The signs test makes sure you can read the signs that control, warn and guide traffic before you drive among them.
Knowing its size and that it is walk-in lets you plan your visit.

scenario.text: Jordan plans to study only the warning signs and walk in for the signs test on Saturday.

reasoning.text: The test covers signs that regulate, warn and direct, and the handbook says to study every sign type.

result.text: Jordan studies the whole signs chapter, then walks in without an appointment.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the signs test needs a booked appointment like the road test.

correction.text: The highway signs test is walk-in; no appointment is needed.

memory_support.text: Fifteen asked, twelve right, walk right in.

prompt.text: A friend has studied only the yellow warning signs before the signs test. What would you advise?

answer.text: Study every sign type in the handbook, not just the warning signs.

rationale.text: The test checks signs that regulate, warn and give directions, and the handbook tells applicants to study all of them.

lines.text: How it is scored and taken.

narration.text: This lesson covers the highway signs test, the first written test on the way to your Wisconsin license. Road signs are the language of the road, and the state wants proof that you can read that language before you drive in traffic. You will learn what the test checks, how many questions it has and how many you need right, whether you need an appointment, and how much of the handbook you should study for it. By the end you should be able to plan your study time and your visit to the customer service center with confidence.

The highway signs test checks whether you can read and understand road signs. The handbook groups them by job. Some signs regulate traffic, telling you what you must or must not do. Some warn drivers about hazards or changes ahead. Others give directions, guiding you toward places and routes. Understanding means more than recognizing a picture: you need to know what each sign asks you to do. That is why the signs chapter later in the handbook describes each sign together with the action it requires, and why the signs test is a separate step from the knowledge test.

The handbook gives the signs test a simple shape. It has fifteen questions, and you must answer twelve of them correctly to pass, which works out to eighty percent. You do not need an appointment; you can walk in for the highway signs test. That makes it easy to fit into your schedule, but walk-in does not mean unprepared. Because the bar is twelve out of fifteen, you can miss only three questions. A few signs you have never studied could be the difference, which leads straight to the handbook's advice about how much to study before you go.

lines.text: Every sign type is fair game.

narration.text: Here is the trap: studying only part of the signs. It is tempting to learn the common ones, such as stop and yield, and skip the rest. The handbook covers every type of sign you may meet, and it tells applicants to study all of them before the signs test. Warning signs, regulatory signs, construction signs, guide signs and railroad signs can all appear. With only three misses allowed out of fifteen, a gap in one family of signs is risky. Treat the signs chapter as the full syllabus for this test, and review it until each sign's meaning comes quickly.

Here is a quick check: a friend has studied only the yellow warning signs before the signs test. What would you advise? Think about what the test covers and what the handbook recommends. The answer is to study every sign type in the handbook, not just the warning signs. The test checks signs that regulate traffic, warn drivers and give directions, and the handbook tells applicants to study all of them. Your friend can still walk in without an appointment, but only after finishing the whole signs chapter, so that twelve out of fifteen feels comfortable rather than lucky.

lines.text: Walk in, but study every sign.

narration.text: Here is the summary. The highway signs test checks whether you can read signs that regulate traffic, warn drivers and give directions. It has fifteen questions, and you need twelve correct, which is eighty percent. You can walk in without an appointment. The handbook covers every sign type and tells you to study all of them before the test, so plan to work through the entire signs chapter. Next you will meet the second written test, the knowledge test on traffic laws, and see how its size, timing and cost compare with the signs test you just learned.

why_how.text: The knowledge test confirms you know Wisconsin traffic laws before you practice on public roads.
Its length, timing and cost decide how and when you should plan to take it.

scenario.text: Priya, age sixteen, plans to take the knowledge test at a center thirty minutes before it closes.

reasoning.text: The test takes about forty-five minutes, so arriving that late risks not finishing before closing.

result.text: Priya arrives earlier in the day, or chooses the paid online option open to her age group.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the signs test and the knowledge test have the same number of questions because they share a pass bar.

correction.text: Both pass at eighty percent, but the signs test is twelve of fifteen and the knowledge test forty of fifty.

memory_support.text: Signs fifteen, laws fifty, both eighty percent.

prompt.text: Someone says the knowledge test is fifteen questions, just like the signs test. How would you correct them?

answer.text: The knowledge test has fifty questions, with forty correct needed; fifteen is the signs test.

rationale.text: The two written tests share the eighty percent bar but not the count: twelve of fifteen for signs, forty of fifty for knowledge.

lines.text: Size, time, cost and the online option.

narration.text: Now for the knowledge test, the second written test on your way to a Wisconsin license. Where the signs test asks whether you can read road signs, the knowledge test asks what you know about Wisconsin traffic laws. In this lesson you will learn its size and pass mark, how it compares with the signs test, how long to set aside for it, and what it costs. You will also learn about an online option open to some younger applicants. These details are easy to mix up, so the lesson points out the comparisons that trip people up most often.

The knowledge test measures what you know about Wisconsin traffic laws, the rules for right-of-way, speed, turning, passing, parking and much more that fill the rest of the handbook. Like the signs test, it needs no appointment, so you can take it without booking ahead. The two written tests differ in subject. The signs test is about reading signs that regulate, warn and direct traffic, while the knowledge test is about the traffic laws themselves. Keeping that difference clear helps you study the right material for each, rather than treating the two as one big written exam.

lines.text: Same eighty percent bar as signs.

narration.text: The handbook says the knowledge test has fifty questions, and you need forty correct answers to pass, which is eighty percent. That is the same percentage as the signs test, but the counts are very different. The signs test is twelve right out of fifteen; the knowledge test is forty right out of fifty. So on the knowledge test you can miss up to ten questions, while on the signs test you can miss only three. Learn the pairs together, fifteen with twelve and fifty with forty, so a question that swaps them does not catch you out.

Expect the knowledge test to take about forty-five minutes. The handbook turns that into practical advice: arrive early enough to finish before the DMV customer service center closes for the day. If you walk in just before closing, you may not have time to complete the test, and you would have to come back. So when you plan your visit, count backward from closing time and leave more than forty-five minutes, especially if you also plan to take the signs test or the vision screening on the same trip. Writing the pairs down once helps.

lines.text: Ages fifteen to seventeen: online, ten dollars.

narration.text: Taking the tests at a DMV customer service center is free, and the DMV website also offers a free practice test you can use while studying. There is one paid option. Applicants between ages fifteen and seventeen may take the knowledge test online instead, for a fee of ten dollars. The handbook mentions that online option only for that age group. So the cost question has a clear answer: in person at a center, free; online, available to fifteen to seventeen year olds, ten dollars. The practice test on the website stays free either way.

Here is the trap that catches many learners. Because both written tests use the same eighty percent bar, people assume they are the same size. They are not. The highway signs test is twelve right out of fifteen, while the knowledge test is forty right out of fifty. A second trap sits in the costs: testing at a center is free, but the online knowledge test for ages fifteen to seventeen costs ten dollars. When a question gives you a number, ask yourself which test it belongs to and whether it describes the in-person or the online route.

lines.text: Is the knowledge test fifteen questions?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: someone tells you the knowledge test is fifteen questions, just like the signs test. How would you correct them? Use the pairs from this lesson. The knowledge test has fifty questions, and forty correct answers are needed to pass. Fifteen is the size of the highway signs test, where twelve correct answers pass. Both tests share the eighty percent bar, which is exactly why the counts get swapped. If you can say both pairs from memory, fifteen and twelve for signs, fifty and forty for knowledge, you are ready for questions that mix them.

To wrap up: the knowledge test measures your knowledge of Wisconsin traffic laws and needs no appointment. It has fifty questions, and forty correct answers, eighty percent, pass it. It takes about forty-five minutes, so arrive early enough to finish before the center closes. Testing at a customer service center is free, the website has a free practice test, and applicants aged fifteen to seventeen may take the knowledge test online for ten dollars. Next you will move from written tests to the skills test, the on-road exam that works quite differently from the walk-in written tests.

why_how.text: The skills test is where you prove in traffic that you can control a vehicle, so it has its own booking rules.
Knowing its other names and the examiner's role prevents confusion when you schedule it.

scenario.text: Sam passes the knowledge test and drives to the center expecting to take the road test on the spot.

reasoning.text: The written tests are walk-in, but the skills test needs an appointment booked on the road test page.

result.text: Sam books a skills test appointment on the DMV website before returning.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the road test can be taken as a walk-in like the written tests.

correction.text: Only the written tests are walk-in; the skills test is appointment-only.

prompt.text: You have finished both written tests. What must you do before you can take the road test?

answer.text: Book a skills test appointment through the road test page of the DMV website.

rationale.text: The written tests are walk-in, but the skills test, also called the road or driving test, is appointment-only.

narration.text: With the written tests behind you, the last step is the skills test. This lesson explains what the skills test is, the different names people use for it, who goes with you during the test, and the one big logistical difference from the written tests: you need an appointment. Many applicants lose time by showing up expecting to drive on the spot, so this lesson is about getting the planning right. In the next lesson you will learn what actually happens and what is graded once your appointment day arrives. Planning ahead keeps the process smooth.

The skills test is a demonstration on public roads that you can keep ordinary, reasonable control of your vehicle. It is not a written exam or a simulation. You will hear it called by three names: the road test, the driving test and the skills test. They all mean the same on-road exam with a DMV examiner. When the handbook or a website uses any of those names, it is talking about this one step. Knowing that saves confusion when you search for how to schedule it or read instructions about preparing for it. The name changes, the exam does not.

lines.text: A DMV examiner goes with you.
Directions are spoken, such as turns.

narration.text: A DMV examiner goes with you on the skills test. The examiner gives spoken directions as you drive, for example telling you to turn left at the next intersection or to make a Y-turn. Your job is to listen, follow each direction safely, and show steady control. The examiner is not there to trick you; the directions let them see how you handle normal driving tasks. Listen to each instruction fully before you act, and if you are unsure, keep driving safely while you think rather than making a sudden move. Calm listening matters as much as skill.

Here is the trap. The two written tests are walk-in, so people assume the skills test works the same way. It does not. Unlike the written tests, the skills test needs an appointment, and you book it through the road test page of the Wisconsin DMV website. Showing up without one means you will not drive that day. A simple way to hold the rule: writing is walk-in, driving is by appointment. Keep this in mind when a question asks which test requires scheduling, because only one of the three tests does. Book early to get a convenient date.

Here is a quick check: you have finished both written tests. What must you do before you can take the road test? Think about which tests are walk-in. The answer is to book a skills test appointment through the road test page of the DMV website. The signs and knowledge tests are walk-in, but the skills test, which is also called the road test or driving test, is appointment-only. Once the appointment is made, your next job is to prepare your car and practice the graded skills, which is exactly what the next lesson covers.

lines.text: Book it on the road test page.

narration.text: In summary, the skills test is a real-world demonstration that you can keep ordinary, reasonable control of your vehicle, and road test, driving test and skills test are three names for the same exam. A DMV examiner rides with you and gives spoken directions such as turns or a Y-turn. Unlike the walk-in written tests, the skills test needs an appointment booked through the road test page of the Wisconsin DMV website. Next you will see what happens on test day, from the vehicle check before you drive to the skills and maneuvers that are graded.

why_how.text: Knowing what is checked lets you prepare both yourself and your car for test day.
Practicing each graded skill and maneuver beforehand is the handbook's own advice.

scenario.text: Alex arrives for the road test in a car with a burned-out brake light and has never used its defroster.

reasoning.text: The examiner inspects the lights before driving, and you should know every control, including the defroster.

result.text: Alex fixes the light and learns the controls before rebooking.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking only the driver is checked on test day.

correction.text: The examiner inspects the car before any driving starts, including the horn, lights and signals, plates, doors and mirrors.

memory_support.text: Car checked first, then turns, lanes, backing.

prompt.text: Your friend practiced stopping at stop signs but never practiced approaching intersections without a stop. Is that enough?

answer.text: No. The road test grades both intersections where you must stop and those you approach without stopping.

rationale.text: Turning and both kinds of intersections are graded, along with lane changes, backing and set maneuvers.

narration.text: This lesson walks you through test day for the skills test. It starts before you drive, with a check of your car, and then covers the controls you should know, the driving skills that are graded, and the set maneuvers you will be asked to perform. The handbook's message is clear: none of this should be new on the day. Everything listed is something you can practice ahead of time with a licensed adult. By the end of this lesson you will have a checklist you can use for your practice drives in the weeks before your appointment.

lines.text: Horn, lights, signals, plates, doors, mirrors.

narration.text: Before the skills test starts, the examiner inspects your car to confirm it is safe to drive. The check covers items such as the horn, the lights and signals, the license plates, the doors, the mirrors and more. This means the car is checked as well as the driver. A burned-out bulb or a mirror that will not adjust can stop the test before it begins. The night before, walk around the car with a helper: test each light and signal, sound the horn, check the plates, and make sure every door and mirror works properly. A quick check prevents a wasted trip.

You should know how to work every vehicle control you might need during the test, such as the headlights, the wipers and the defroster. Weather can change during a drive, and the examiner expects you to respond without fumbling. Knowing where these controls are is part of being ready for the road test, not an optional extra. If you are borrowing a car for the test, spend time in it beforehand. Practice switching on the headlights, running the wipers at different speeds and clearing a fogged windshield, so your hands find each control without looking away from the road.

The skills test grades turning, intersections where you must stop, and the approach to intersections where no stop is required. It also grades driving through business or residential areas, changing lanes, and backing up. That is a broad list, and each item is everyday driving done carefully: checking around you, signaling, controlling speed and choosing the right lane position. Plan practice drives that include each one. Drive through a neighborhood and a shopping district, change lanes on a multi-lane road, and practice backing in an empty lot until it feels routine.

Along with general driving, the test includes set maneuvers such as a Y-turn, a roadside stop and start, and parking, so practice each one beforehand. The Y-turn shows up twice in the handbook's description: as an example of a spoken direction from the examiner and again in the list of maneuvers. That double mention is a hint that you will very likely be asked to do one. The roadside stop and start checks that you can pull over and rejoin traffic safely, and parking checks your control at low speed. Practice all three in quiet places first.

Here is the trap. Learners practice stopping at stop signs and think intersections are covered. But the road test grades intersections both ways: the ones where you must stop and the ones you approach without a stop. At an intersection with no stop required, the examiner still watches how you scan, adjust your speed and stay ready to yield. So build both into your practice. Approach intersections with no sign or with a green light just as carefully as stop-sign corners, looking left, right and ahead before you commit to going through.

Here is a quick check: your friend practiced stopping at stop signs but never practiced approaching intersections without a stop. Is that enough for the road test? Think about the list of graded skills. The answer is no. The road test grades both intersections where you must stop and those you approach without stopping. It also grades turning, driving through business or residential areas, changing lanes, backing up and the set maneuvers. Your friend should add no-stop intersections to the practice plan, along with every other item on that list, before test day arrives.

lines.text: Inspect the car, know the controls.

narration.text: To finish: before the skills test the examiner inspects your car, including the horn, lights and signals, plates, doors and mirrors. Know how to work every control you might need, such as headlights, wipers and the defroster. The test grades turning, must-stop and no-stop intersections, business or residential driving, lane changes and backing, plus set maneuvers such as a Y-turn, a roadside stop and start, and parking. The DMV website has more guidance, and the handbook's advice is simple: practice every listed skill before test day so nothing feels new.
